```{r setup}
# Loading pre-fitted saves ~5 minutes of render time
models_imputed <- readRDS(here::here("data", "models_imputed.rds"))
mod_e_all      <- models_imputed$all
mod_e_disadv   <- models_imputed$disadvantaged
mod_e_nondisadv <- models_imputed$non_disadvantaged

# LA ranks for Brighton and Hove from the fitted models (1 = best), so the
# ranks quoted in the text cannot drift from the models they come from.
la_rank <- function(model) {
  re <- lme4::ranef(model)[["LANAME:gor_name"]]
  d  <- tibble(grp = rownames(re), eff = re[["(Intercept)"]]) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(la = sub(":.*$", "", grp)) %>%
    dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(eff)) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(rank = dplyr::row_number())
  bh <- d %>% dplyr::filter(grepl("Brighton", la))
  list(rank = bh$rank, n = nrow(d))
}
rk_all <- la_rank(mod_e_all)
rk_dis <- la_rank(mod_e_disadv)
rk_non <- la_rank(mod_e_nondisadv)

# ---- Helper functions ----
relabel_terms <- function(term) {
  case_when(
    term == "(Intercept)" ~ "(Intercept)",
    term == "log(PTFSM6CLA1A)" ~ "log(% FSM)",
    term == "log(PERCTOT)" ~ "log(% Absence)",
    term == "log(PNUMEAL)" ~ "log(% EAL)",
    term == "ks2_c" ~ "Mean KS2 Prior Attainment",
    term == "gorard_segregation" ~ "Gorard Segregation",
    term == "ADMPOL_PTOTHER NON SEL" ~ "Admissions: Other non-selective (ref: non-sel. in highly sel. area)",
    term == "ADMPOL_PTSEL" ~ "Admissions: Selective (ref: non-sel. in highly sel. area)",
    term == "remained_in_the_same_school" ~ "Teacher Retention",
    term == "teachers_on_leadership_pay_range_percent" ~ "Leadership Pay %",
    term == "log(average_number_of_days_taken)" ~ "log(Teacher Sickness)",
    TRUE ~ term
  )
}

ordinal_suffix <- function(n) {
  suffix <- case_when(
    n %% 100 %in% c(11, 12, 13) ~ "th",
    n %% 10 == 1 ~ "st",
    n %% 10 == 2 ~ "nd",
    n %% 10 == 3 ~ "rd",
    TRUE ~ "th"
  )
  paste0(n, suffix)
}

# ---- Choice: what families respond to --------------------------------
DECAY_A <- acc$pref$decay
ch_prefs <- fpan$factsheets %>%
  filter(name != "Total", year >= max(year) - 4) %>%
  group_by(name) %>%
  summarise(p1 = mean(pref1), p2 = mean(pref2), p3 = mean(pref3), .groups = "drop") %>%
  inner_join(oi$attract %>% select(urn, name), by = "name")
cd <- os$choice %>%
  select(urn, school, pan, att8, va) %>%
  inner_join(ch_prefs %>% select(-name), by = "urn") %>%
  mutate(short = short_sch(school),
         wpp = (p1 + DECAY_A * p2 + DECAY_A^2 * p3) / pan)
fit_att8 <- lm(log(wpp) ~ att8, data = cd)
fit_va   <- lm(log(wpp) ~ va, data = cd)
r2_att8  <- summary(fit_att8)$r.squared
r2_va    <- summary(fit_va)$r.squared
att8_pct <- 100 * (exp(coef(fit_att8)[["att8"]]) - 1)
cd_of <- function(s, col) cd[[col]][cd$short == s]
```

```{r brighton-ai-extras}
# ---- The open-allocation question, read off the model ----------------

# each setting, so the slide quotes the model rather than an opinion.

# ---- The Longhill policy ladder, as demonstrated live ----------------
# Read off the simulator for 2026 entry, one control changed at a time.
steps <- tibble::tibble(
  step  = factor(1:4),
  label = c("Today", "Families read value added",
            "+ Elm Grove, Whitehawk back", "+ value added doubled"),
  intake = c(90, 106, 140, 197),
  pct    = c(43, 50, 67, 94),
  dep    = c(3.4, 2.5, -1.9, -2.2),
  seg    = c(0.117, 0.127, 0.176, 0.188))
st <- function(i, col) steps[[col]][i]

# ---- The cohort decline, in one number -------------------------------
y7_peak   <- max(rc$secondary_city$y7_offers)
y7_peak_y <- rc$secondary_city$year[which.max(rc$secondary_city$y7_offers)]
y7_now    <- rc$secondary_city$y7_offers[which.max(rc$secondary_city$year)]
y7_end    <- rc$projection$central[which.max(rc$projection$entry_year)]
y7_end_y  <- max(rc$projection$entry_year)
y7_drop   <- round((y7_peak - y7_end) / 10) * 10
```

# A thorny local problem {background-color="#17204d"}

## The Brighton and Hove Secondary School System

```{r catchments-map}

# ---- Load catchment boundaries ----
optionZ <- st_read(
  here::here("data", "optionZ_Mar25.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
) %>%
  st_transform(4326)

# ---- Catchment colour palette ----
catchment_colours <- c(
  "BACA"              = "#e41a1c",
  "HoveBlatchington"  = "#377eb8",
  "Longhill"          = "#4daf4a",
  "PACA"              = "#984ea3",
  "Patcham"           = "#ff7f00",
  "VarndeanStringer"  = "#a65628"
)
pal_catch <- colorFactor(
  palette = unname(catchment_colours),
  domain = names(catchment_colours)
)

# ---- Catchment labels ----
catchment_labels <- c(
  "BACA"              = "BACA (Brighton Aldridge)",
  "HoveBlatchington"  = "Hove Park / Blatchington Mill",
  "Longhill"          = "Longhill",
  "PACA"              = "PACA (Portslade Aldridge)",
  "Patcham"           = "Patcham",
  "VarndeanStringer"  = "Varndean / Dorothy Stringer"
)

# ---- School locations ----
bh_map_data <- bh_latest %>%
  filter(!is.na(easting), !is.na(northing)) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("easting", "northing"), crs = 27700) %>%
  st_transform(4326)

map_coords <- st_coordinates(bh_map_data)
bh_map_data$lon <- map_coords[, 1]
bh_map_data$lat <- map_coords[, 2]

# ---- School logo paths (relative to project root) ----
logo_paths <- c(
  "Blatchington Mill School"                = "output/school_logos/blatchington_mill.png",
  "Brighton Aldridge Community Academy"      = "output/school_logos/brighton_aldridge.png",
  "Cardinal Newman Catholic School"          = "output/school_logos/cardinal_newman.png",
  "Dorothy Stringer School"                  = "output/school_logos/dorothy_stringer.png",
  "Hove Park School and Sixth Form Centre"   = "output/school_logos/hove_park.png",
  "King's School"                            = "output/school_logos/kings_school.png",
  "Longhill High School"                     = "output/school_logos/longhill_high.png",
  "Patcham High School"                      = "output/school_logos/patcham_high.png",
  "Portslade Aldridge Community Academy"     = "output/school_logos/portslade_aldridge.png",
  "Varndean School"                          = "output/school_logos/varndean.png"
)

# ---- Build the leaflet map ----
m_orient <- leaflet(width = "100%", height = 480) %>%
  add_basemap() %>%
  addPolygons(
    data = optionZ,
    group = "Catchment boundaries",
    fillColor = ~pal_catch(catchment),
    fillOpacity = 0.12,
    color = ~pal_catch(catchment),
    weight = 2.5,
    opacity = 0.8,
    label = ~catchment_labels[catchment],
    highlightOptions = highlightOptions(
      weight = 4, fillOpacity = 0.25, bringToFront = FALSE
    )
  )


# ---- Where the children actually live ----------------------------------
# One circle per postcode, sized by the number of households with
# dependent children and coloured by IDACI decile (1 = most deprived
# tenth of England). Rebuilt from the 2021 Census postcode tables and
# ONSPD centroids; the same layer as the Brighton consultation work.
# Drawn before the schools so the logos stay readable over it.
bh_pop <- readRDS(here::here("data", "bh_postcode_population.rds"))

pal_idaci <- colorFactor(
  palette = "RdYlBu",
  domain = sort(unique(bh_pop$idaci_decile))
)

m_orient <- m_orient %>%
  addCircleMarkers(
    data = bh_pop,
    group = "Where the children live",
    radius = ~sqrt(hh_dep_ch) * 1.5,
    fillColor = ~pal_idaci(idaci_decile),
    fillOpacity = 0.55,
    stroke = FALSE,
    label = ~sprintf(
      "%s - %.0f households with children, %.0f households in all, IDACI decile %.0f",
      postcode, hh_dep_ch, total_hh, idaci_decile
    )
  ) %>%
  addLegend(
    pal = pal_idaci,
    values = sort(unique(bh_pop$idaci_decile)),
    title = "IDACI decile<br><span style='font-weight:normal'>1 = most deprived</span>",
    opacity = 1,
    position = "bottomright"
  )
# Add each school as a dot + logo marker
for (i in seq_len(nrow(bh_map_data))) {
  sch_name <- bh_map_data$SCHNAME[i]
  sch_lon  <- bh_map_data$lon[i]
  sch_lat  <- bh_map_data$lat[i]

  popup_html <- sprintf(
    "<b>%s</b><br>ATT8: %.1f | FSM: %.1f%% | Absence: %.1f%%",
    sch_name,
    bh_map_data$ATT8SCR[i],
    bh_map_data$PTFSM6CLA1A[i],
    bh_map_data$PERCTOT[i]
  )

  m_orient <- m_orient %>%
    addCircleMarkers(
      lng = sch_lon, lat = sch_lat,
      radius = 5, fillColor = "#333333", fillOpacity = 0.9,
      group = "Schools",
      color = "white", weight = 1.5,
      popup = popup_html
    )

  logo_file <- logo_paths[sch_name]
  if (!is.na(logo_file) && file.exists(logo_file)) {
    logo_b64 <- knitr::image_uri(logo_file)
    logo_icon <- makeIcon(
      iconUrl = logo_b64,
      iconWidth = 36, iconHeight = 36,
      iconAnchorX = -4, iconAnchorY = 40
    )
    m_orient <- m_orient %>%
      addMarkers(
        lng = sch_lon, lat = sch_lat,
        icon = logo_icon,
        group = "Schools",
        popup = popup_html
      )
  }
}

# ---- CoMArt (Closed 2005) ----
comart_lon <- -0.099449
comart_lat <- 50.823301
comart_popup <- "<b>CoMArt (Closed 2005)</b>"

m_orient <- m_orient %>%

# Legend — use HTML labels with inline coloured squares for clean alignment
legend_html <- paste0(
  '<div style="font-size: 12px; line-height: 1.6;">',
  paste0(
    '<div style="display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 6px;">',
    '<span style="display: inline-block; width: 14px; height: 14px; ',
    'background:', unname(catchment_colours), '; ',

  ),

m_orient <- m_orient %>%
  addControl(
    html = paste0(
      '<div style="background: white; padding: 8px 12px; ',
      'border-radius: 4px; box-shadow: 0 1px 5px rgba(0,0,0,0.3); ',
      'font-family: sans-serif;">',
      '<div style="font-weight: bold; margin-bottom: 4px; font-size: 12px;">',
      '2025/26 Catchment Boundaries</div>',
      legend_html,

# Frame on where the children are, not on the full reach of the catchments:
# PACA's boundary runs west past Shoreham and would otherwise set the view.
bb <- as.numeric(sf::st_bbox(bh_pop))
m_orient <- m_orient %>%
  fitBounds(bb[1], bb[2], bb[3], bb[4])

# Let the room turn each layer off. Collapsed = FALSE so the options are
# visible on the slide rather than hidden behind a hover target.
m_orient <- m_orient %>%
  addLayersControl(
    overlayGroups = c("Where the children live", "Catchment boundaries",
                      "Schools", "CoMArt (closed 2005)"),
    options = layersControlOptions(collapsed = FALSE),
    position = "topleft"
  )

if (knitr::is_html_output()) {
  m_orient
} else {
  # Static map for PDF output
  ggplot() +
    geom_sf(data = optionZ, aes(fill = catchment), alpha = 0.15,
            colour = NA, show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_sf(data = optionZ, aes(colour = catchment), fill = NA,
            linewidth = 0.6, show.legend = TRUE) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = catchment_colours, labels = catchment_labels,
                      aesthetics = c("fill", "colour"), name = "Catchment") +
    geom_point(data = as.data.frame(bh_map_data),
               aes(x = lon, y = lat), size = 2, colour = "#333333") +
    geom_text_repel(data = as.data.frame(bh_map_data),
                    aes(x = lon, y = lat, label = SCHNAME),
                    size = 2, max.overlaps = 15, force = 3,
                    segment.colour = "grey50", segment.size = 0.3) +
    # CoMArt
    geom_point(aes(x = comart_lon, y = comart_lat),
               size = 2, colour = "#e41a1c") +
    annotate("text", x = comart_lon + 0.005, y = comart_lat,
             label = "CoMArt (Closed 2005)", size = 2, colour = "#e41a1c", hjust = 0) +
    theme_void(base_size = 10) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom",
          legend.text = element_text(size = 7))
}
```

::: {style="font-size:0.74em; color:#666688; text-align:center; margin-top:-0.4rem;"}
Ten schools, six catchments. **A (mostly) closed system with hard
edges:** every child the council places has to go somewhere. Some
pockets of deprivation in East of the city.
:::

## Two years ago, the argument was about attainment and 'fairness' {.smaller}

The 2024 reforms changed catchment boundaries, introduced a free school
meals priority, and held back **5% of places at central schools for
"open allocation"** — children from anywhere in the city - potentially
forcing some children to attend schools outside of their catchment where
schools over-subscribed.

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**The council's stated aim**

Reduce the concentration of disadvantaged pupils in a few schools, and
so *narrow the attainment gap*. Latterly - increase 'fairness'.

**What I went and checked**

Every secondary school in England, five years of data, a model of what
actually predicts a GCSE cohort's results.
:::

:::: {.column width="50%"}
::: key-finding
**What the evidence says**

- Only about **15%** of the variation in a child's GCSE results is down
  to the school. The rest is the child, the family, and what happened
  before they arrived.
- **Absence is biggest issue in the city and most associated with
  attainment** but was not in the consultation at all.
- For disadvantaged pupils, concentration is **not** the harm it is
  assumed to be. Nationally, once absence and prior attainment are
  accounted for, they do slightly *better* in schools with more
  disadvantaged pupils.
:::
::::
::::::

***Is it fair to promise benefits not supported by the evidence, ignore
the dis-benefits and knowingly makes the lives of a few unlucky children
worse in the process?***



## But while we were arguing, the ground was moving {.smaller}

```{r cohort-plot}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.8
y7 <- rc$secondary_city; recp <- rc$reception_city; proj <- rc$projection
ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(data = proj, aes(entry_year, ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = BAD, alpha = 0.18) +
  geom_line(data = recp, aes(year, rec_offers), colour = "#2c7fb8", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_line(data = y7, aes(year, y7_offers), colour = INK, linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_line(data = proj, aes(entry_year, central), colour = BAD, linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "22") +
  annotate("text", x = min(recp$year) + 0.3, y = max(recp$rec_offers) * 1.03,
           label = "Reception offers", colour = "#2c7fb8", hjust = 0, size = 4.4) +
  annotate("text", x = min(y7$year) + 0.3, y = min(y7$y7_offers) * 0.93,
           label = "Year 7 offers", colour = INK, hjust = 0, size = 4.4, fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("text", x = max(proj$entry_year) - 0.2, y = max(proj$hi) * 1.06,
           label = "Projected from children\nalready in primary school",
           colour = BAD, hjust = 1, size = 4) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma(), limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Offers",
```

::: {style="font-size:0.84em"}
Year 7 entry peaked at **`r fmt_n(y7_peak)` in `r y7_peak_y`**. By
**`r y7_end_y`** it is projected at about **`r fmt_n(y7_end)`** —
roughly **`r fmt_n(y7_drop)` fewer children** entering secondary school
each year. More than the entire intake of two of the city's large
schools.
:::

## Schools are funded per pupil {.smaller}

```{r reserves-plot}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5.0
fex <- sfin$exposure |> dplyr::mutate(short = short_sch(name))
ord <- fex |> dplyr::arrange(reserve_pct) |> dplyr::pull(name)
rp <- sfin$panel |> dplyr::mutate(school = factor(short_sch(name), short_sch(ord)),
                                  neg = pmin(reserve_pct, 0))
ggplot(rp, aes(year, reserve_pct)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = neg, ymax = 0), fill = "#d03b3b", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9, colour = INK) + geom_point(size = 1.2, colour = INK) +
  facet_wrap(~ school, ncol = 5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = sort(unique(rp$year)),
                     labels = function(x) paste0(substr(x, 3, 4), "/", substr(x + 1, 3, 4))) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Reserve as a share of income",
       title = "Revenue reserves, worst first. Red shading is a school in deficit.",
       subtitle = "DfE school income and expenditure returns") +
  theme_bhs(12) + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 7))
```

::: {style="font-size:0.84em"}
Fewer children means less money. Less money means fewer subjects, bigger
classes, a worse offer — and so fewer children. **Decline is
self-reinforcing, and it does not land evenly.**
:::

## It is landing on one school first {.smaller}

```{r drift-plot}

#| fig-height: 4.9
fs <- fpan$factsheets |>

ends <- fs |> dplyr::group_by(school, lh) |> dplyr::filter(year == max(year)) |> dplyr::ungroup()

ggplot(fs, aes(year, off_total, group = school)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 210, linetype = "31", colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.4) +
  annotate("text", x = max(fs$year) + 0.4, y = 210, hjust = 0, size = 3.4,
           colour = "grey45", label = "210 places") +
  geom_line(data = dplyr::filter(fs, !lh), colour = "grey78", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = dplyr::filter(fs, lh), colour = BAD, linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_point(data = dplyr::filter(fs, lh), colour = BAD, size = 2) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(
    data = dplyr::filter(ends, !lh), aes(label = school),
    size = 3.2, colour = "grey45", direction = "y", hjust = 0,
    nudge_x = 0.4, segment.colour = "grey80", segment.size = 0.3,
    max.overlaps = 20, xlim = c(max(fs$year) + 0.3, NA)) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(
    data = dplyr::filter(ends, lh), aes(label = school),
    size = 4.2, fontface = "bold", colour = BAD, direction = "y", hjust = 0,
    nudge_x = 0.4, segment.colour = BAD, segment.size = 0.3,
    xlim = c(max(fs$year) + 0.3, NA)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2010, 2026, 4),
                     limits = c(min(fs$year), max(fs$year) + 4.2)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Children allocated a place",
       title = "Longhill, against every other school in the city",

```

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}
The city placed **1,900 children in 2010 and 2,250 in 2026** — it grew.
Over the same years **Longhill fell from 239 to 81**. Now the cohort
turns down, and the school at the edge of the city gets the fall first.
:::

## So here is the actual problem {.smaller}

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="54%"}
In ten years this city has to run a school system for roughly
**`r fmt_n(y7_drop)` fewer children a year** than it has now.

That means, unavoidably, some combination of:

- schools getting **smaller**,
- schools **closing**,
- **catchments** redrawn,
- or a lot of **half-empty buildings** quietly going bankrupt.

Every one of those makes somebody's journey longer, or takes a school
out of somebody's community.
:::

:::: {.column width="46%"}
::: key-finding
**And there is no long-term plan.**

What exists is a sequence of individual consultations — each on a single
option, each argued about on its own, each decided before the next one
is proposed.

Nobody has published an account of how the whole system behaves, so
nobody can say what any one of these decisions does to the others.
:::

Hopefully not a conspiracy. It is just **hard**, and nobody had the
tools to think strategically.
::::
::::::

# We need to be able to try things {background-color="#17204d"}

## Problems with Piecemeal Policy {.smaller}

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**How it works now**

- A consultation proposes some changes and provides little supporting
  evidence.
- People respond for or against.
- The council does what it wants anyway.
- Twelve months later the next consultation arrives, and nobody has
  checked what the last one did.

The system, meanwhile, is **interacting**. Move a catchment and demand
shifts at four schools. Cut an admission number and the children do not
vanish — they turn up somewhere else.
:::

:::: {.column width="50%"}
**How it could work**

- Ask *"what if?"* twenty times before lunch.
- Stack simulated policies and watch them compound over time.
- Find the combinations that work, and the ones that cost somebody
  something.
- Share this knowledge with everyone who is being asked to have an
  opinion on a proposal in a consultation

::: key-finding
Run the experiment **in silico**, where being wrong costs nothing —
instead of running it on a cohort of eleven-year-olds, where being wrong
costs them a place in a local school.
:::
::::
::::::

# The tool {background-color="#17204d"}

## What it is {.smaller}

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
| The thing                        | Scale                  |
|:---------------------------------|:-----------------------|
| Strategic analysis of the system | 9,712 lines of Quarto  |
| The model and data assembly      | \~7,400 lines of R     |
| An interactive policy simulator  | \~3,000 lines of Shiny |
| Commits across six repositories  | 805                    |

Everything is **open**: the code, the data sources, the model, the
write-up. Every number on every slide traces back to a line of code and
a published source.
:::

:::: {.column width="48%"}
![](slides_assets/simulator-starting.png){.nostretch width="100%"}

::: {style="font-size:0.74em; color:#666688;"}
Sliders for attractiveness, a dropdown for what families read, controls
for catchments, admission numbers, school locations and open allocation.
Hit go and the whole city re-allocates.
:::
::::
::::::

## Where the data comes from {.smaller}

::::::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
**Nothing here is private.** No pupil records, no data-sharing
agreement, no permission required. All of it is published, and ***most
of it is published badly.***

- DfE performance tables and the statistics API — attainment, absence,
  intake, workforce, finance 🤘
- Council **allocation factsheets**, 2010 onwards — preferences and
  offers, school by school, year by year (dug out from buried URLs and
  collated by me 😭)
- The 2021 **Census** — where children actually live, postcode by
  postcode 🤘
- **OpenStreetMap** road network and the real **bus timetable (GTFS)**
- Catchment boundaries (traced by me 😭), and one **Freedom of
  Information request** 💪
:::

::::: {.column width="40%"}
::: key-finding
Data processing and curation from a dozen sources that do not share a key, do not share a year, do not share a school name, and change their format every two years, just the sort of thing Claude AI excels at.

Exactly the grinding, careful, enormously tedious work that has
historically eaten the entire budget of a project like this.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.8em; color:#666688; margin-top:0.8rem;"}
Everything open and downloadable from my github
:::
:::::
:::::::

## The model underneath {.smaller}

A **spatial interaction model** — the same family used for commuting,
migration and retail catchments since the 1970s. It predicts how many
children flow from each neighbourhood to each school.

$$T_{ij} \;=\; A_i\,O_i\;\;W_j\;\;c_{ij}^{-\beta}\;\;e^{\gamma_h}\;\;C_j^{\delta}$$

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
| Term           | What it is                                    |
|:---------------|:----------------------------------------------|
| $T_{ij}$       | children from neighbourhood $i$ to school $j$ |
| $O_i$          | children living in $i$ — 195 neighbourhoods   |
| $W_j$          | how attractive school $j$ is                  |
| $c_{ij}$       | bus-and-walk journey time, $i$ to $j$         |
| $e^{\gamma_h}$ | the catchment bonus                           |
| $C_j$          | how much competition $j$ has nearby           |
| $A_i$          | the balancing term                            |
:::

:::: {.column width="48%"}
It is **production-constrained**: $A_i$ forces every child living
somewhere to end up somewhere. The model never invents or loses
children; it only decides where they go.

::: key-finding
That is what makes it useful for policy. Close a school, move one, cut
its admission number — and the children **reappear somewhere else**, and
the model tells you where.
:::
::::
::::::

## $W_j$ - What makes a school attractive? {.smaller}

```{r choice}
#| fig-height: 4.6
pl <- function(x, xlab, r2, colr) {
  ggplot(cd, aes(.data[[x]], wpp)) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, colour = colr,
                linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.9) +
    geom_point(size = 3.2, colour = colr) +
    geom_text_repel(aes(label = short), size = 3.3, seed = 3, colour = INK) +
    scale_y_log10() +
    labs(x = xlab, y = if (x == "att8") "Preferences per place (log)" else NULL,
         subtitle = sprintf("R² = %.2f", r2)) +
    theme_slide
}
(pl("att8", "Headline Attainment 8", r2_att8, BAD) |
 pl("va", "Value added (what the school contributes)", r2_va, "#2166ac")) +
  plot_annotation(title = "Demand follows the headline score, not what a school adds",
                  subtitle = sprintf("Ten city schools, five-year means. Each point of Attainment 8 goes with about %.0f%% more preferences per place.", att8_pct),
                  theme = theme_slide)
```

::: {style="font-size:0.62em; color:#555;"}

And the council's own [admissions guide](`r GUIDE`) tells parents to look at exam results and Ofsted reports. A school with a more disadvantaged intake posts a lower headline score, so fewer families 
choose it, so its intake gets more disadvantaged, so the score falls again. **The advice works against the policy.**

:::

## What cost - $c_{ij}$ - actually means {.smaller}

```{r fig-route-baca}
#| fig-cap: "One neighbourhood in the Stringer/Varndean catchment to BACA. Walking legs orange and dashed, bus legs blue. Routed on the real timetable at 08:00."
gr <- bh_data("guide_routes.rds")
BACA <- "Brighton Aldridge Community Academy"

rt   <- gr$summary |> dplyr::filter(school == BACA)
legs <- gr$legs    |> dplyr::filter(school == BACA) |>
  dplyr::mutate(mode = ifelse(leg_mode == "WALK", "Walk", "Bus"))
bus  <- legs |> dplyr::filter(mode == "Bus")

sch <- inp$schools |> dplyr::filter(city) |>
  sf::st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE)
catch_g <- sf::st_read(here::here("data", "optionZ_Mar25.geojson"), quiet = TRUE) |>
  sf::st_transform(4326)
bb <- sf::st_bbox(legs)

leaflet(width = "100%", height = 440) |>
  add_basemap() |>
  addPolygons(data = catch_g, fill = FALSE, color = "#555555",
              weight = 1, opacity = 0.45) |>
  addPolylines(data = dplyr::filter(legs, mode == "Walk"), color = "#e08214",
               weight = 5, opacity = 0.9, dashArray = "6 6", label = ~"Walk") |>
  addPolylines(data = dplyr::filter(legs, mode == "Bus"), color = "#2166ac",
               weight = 5, opacity = 0.9, label = ~paste("Bus", route)) |>
  addCircleMarkers(data = dplyr::filter(sch, name != BACA), radius = 3,
                   color = "#777777", weight = 1, fillColor = "#cccccc",
                   fillOpacity = 0.9, label = ~short) |>
  addCircleMarkers(data = dplyr::filter(sch, name == BACA), radius = 8,
                   color = "#111111", weight = 2, fillColor = "#ffffff",
                   fillOpacity = 1, label = ~short) |>
  addCircleMarkers(lng = gr$origin$lon, lat = gr$origin$lat, radius = 8,
                   color = "#111111", weight = 2, fillColor = "#b2182b",
                   fillOpacity = 1, label = "Home") |>
  fitBounds(bb[["xmin"]] - 0.004, bb[["ymin"]] - 0.003,
            bb[["xmax"]] + 0.004, bb[["ymax"]] + 0.003)
```

::: {style="font-size:0.74em"}
**`r sprintf("%.1f", rt$km)` km as the crow flies.
`r round(rt$route_minutes)` minutes, `r rt$legs` legs, two buses — the
`r rt$services` — and `r rt$changes` change.** Every one of the
`r format(195 * 15, big.mark = ",")` origin-school pairs in the model is routed like this, on the real timetable. That is what $c_{ij}$ is.
:::

## Three things it had to learn {.smaller}

::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="54%"}
Fitted to the council's own published allocations, not assumed:

**Distance decay,** $\beta = 1.7$ — how steeply demand falls as a school
gets further away. And $c_{ij}$ is not crow-flies: every one of the
`r format(195 * 15, big.mark = ",")` origin–school pairs is routed on
the **real bus timetable at 08:00**.

**The catchment pull,** $\gamma_h$ — fitted **separately for every
catchment**, because they do not behave alike.

**Competition,** $\delta = 0.3$ — whether being surrounded by rivals
helps a school or hurts it.

::: key-finding
Living in the catchment multiplies the odds by **2.7 times** at Brighton
Aldridge and **13.5 times** at Stringer and Varndean. One policy doing
five times as much work in one part of the city as another.
:::
::::

:::: {.column width="46%"}
::: {style="text-align:center; line-height:0.8; margin-top:-0.4rem;"}
![](slides_assets/fig-beta-curve.png){width="56%"
style="display:block; margin:0 auto;"}
![](slides_assets/fig-gamma-map.png){width="56%"
style="display:block; margin:0 auto;"}
![](slides_assets/fig-cj-map.png){width="56%"
style="display:block; margin:0 auto;"}
:::
::::
:::::::

## Does it work? - Hell Yeah! {.smaller}

::::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
It reproduces the September 2026 allocations with an **R² of 0.95**.

More importantly, it has been given tests it **could have failed**, on
numbers that did not exist when it was built:

- A Freedom of Information request produced the confirmed September
  position by admission priority. The model had never seen it.
- Longhill's modelled 2026 intake of **90** sits inside the FOI's actual
  range of **91 to 99**.
:::

::::: {.column width="50%"}
::: key-finding
And it gets things wrong in ways I can name. It **over-predicts the
schools that are hard to get into** by about 16 children — because it
reproduces the *allocation*, and the allocation overstates where
children finally end up.

A model you cannot criticise is not a model. It is a press release.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.8em; margin-top:0.7rem;"}
All of it is written up, failures included, in a technical guide that
audits every term.
:::
:::::
:::::::

# How this got built {background-color="#17204d"}

## Fifty years of models. Five months of building. {.smaller}

::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="52%"}
- The model underpinning the simulator is a development of Newton's Gravity equation.
- The Spatial Interaction Model was first popularised by Sir Alan Wilson in 1970 and used successfully to solve spatial problems in cities for decades
- I've been building these models for 20-years. I had a hand-written prototype of this one on my computer from 2024, and a routing pipeline to go with it.
-  What I did not have was **a month of uninterrupted time** to turn it
into something a city could use. I was never going to get one.

::: key-finding
So I did it with **Claude Code**, in bursts, in evenings, between
everything else. Counted from the logs: **1,277 instructions** from me,
**13,451 actions** back, over **69 working days** spread across five
months.
:::
::::

:::: {.column width="48%"}
```{r timeline-plot}
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 4.3
ggplot(rec, aes(day)) +
  geom_col(aes(y = tool_calls), fill = BRIGHT, width = 1.9, alpha = 0.9) +
  geom_line(aes(y = instructions * 10), colour = WARM, linewidth = 0.9, linetype = "31") +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Actions by Claude per day",
                     sec.axis = sec_axis(~ . / 10, name = "My instructions per day")) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%b") +
  labs(x = NULL, title = "Bursty, and accelerating",
       subtitle = "Bars: Claude. Dashed line: me.") +
  theme_talk(12) +
  theme(axis.title.y.right = element_text(colour = WARM),
        axis.title.y.left  = element_text(colour = BRIGHT))
```

::: {style="font-size:0.72em; color:#666688;"}
The April to July work is a different project — a national attainment
model. The city system model itself starts on **8 September** and is
finished eighteen days later.
:::
::::
:::::::

## The division of labour {.smaller}

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="49%"}
**What I brought to the party**

- A working prototype ("Brightopia"), built by hand in 2024
- Twenty years of knowing *which terms matter* — attractiveness,
  distance decay, competing destinations
- Knowledge of the school system, and of the city's politics
- A critical eye to review the outputs
- **Knowing when an answer was wrong**
- Every decision about what to do next
:::

::: {.column width="2%"}
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
**What Claude brought**

- Scale: a prototype turned into a calibrated, audited system
- Data wrangling across a dozen awkward published sources
- Shiny, deployment, rendering, version control
- Debugging, and the patience for it
- Documentation written as it went
- The willingness to **redo all of it** when one assumption changed
- Speed, coding abilities, technical prowess
:::
::::::

::: key-finding
I knew what to ask for and what to examine **because I had built a smaller version of it myself**. The ***Human in the loop*** was vital in this process - asking the right questions, giving the right instructions, reviewing the outputs and forcing iteration
:::

## What AI has changed for me {.smaller}

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
- **It does not replace knowing things.** 
- Every moment that mattered in this project turned on domain knowledge I had and it did not. 
- Several times it produced something plausible but not quite right, and the only reason it got caught was my experience.

- **It does collapse the cost of trying.** 
- Each scenario I tested would have been a week of work. I would have tested a couple, but I tested twenty-odd.
:::

:::: {.column width="50%"}
::: key-finding
**The bottleneck moved.** It is no longer implementation.

It is **knowing which question is worth asking** — and that is a
distinctly human, distinctly local, distinctly collective thing.

Which is more or less the whole argument of this talk.
:::
::::
::::::

# Let me show you {background-color="#1f4599"}

## Live demo {.smaller}

<https://adamdennett-bh-school-system.share.connect.posit.cloud/>

::::::: columns
::: {.column width="65%"}
**What I am going to do:** take the school in the most trouble, and pull
one lever at a time.

1.  **Today.** Longhill is modelled at **`r st(1,"intake")` of 210
    places** — and that matches reality.
2.  **What if families read value added** instead of the headline score?
    One dropdown. Nothing about any school changes.
3.  **What if we moved it** to the top of Elm Grove, where a school was
    proposed a few years ago — and put **Whitehawk back** into its
    catchment, as it was before 2004?
4.  **What if it taught like BACA** — the school down the road with a
    comparably disadvantaged intake and the best value added in the
    city?

Then push the whole thing forward to **2035**, with the falling cohort,
and see which schools are still viable.
:::

::::: {.column width="35%"}
::: key-finding
The point is not any one of these. **No single policy does much on its
own.** That is exactly why they keep dying at consultation — each one,
judged alone, looks like it is not worth the trouble.

Watch what happens when you **stack them**.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.78em; color:#666688; margin-top:0.8rem;"}
Nothing here harms a single child. That is the whole argument for doing
it this way round.
:::
:::::
:::::::

## What the demo showed {visibility="uncounted"}

::::::: columns
::: {.column width="56%"}
```{r ladder-plot}
#| fig-width: 7.0
#| fig-height: 4.6
sl <- steps |>
  dplyr::mutate(lab = stringr::str_wrap(label, 18),
                lab = factor(lab, levels = stringr::str_wrap(label, 18)))
ggplot(sl, aes(lab, pct, group = 1)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 100, linetype = "31", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1, colour = BAD) +
  geom_point(size = 3.6, colour = BAD) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%d%%", pct)), vjust = -1.1, size = 4.4, colour = INK) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 112)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Longhill's places filled",
       title = "No single lever fills Longhill. Four together nearly do.",
       subtitle = "2026 entry. Each step keeps the one before it.") +
  theme_bhs(12) + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 9))
```
:::

::::: {.column width="44%"}
::: {style="font-size:0.86em"}
Each step is modest: **`r st(2,"pct")-st(1,"pct")` points, then
`r st(3,"pct")-st(2,"pct")`, then `r st(4,"pct")-st(3,"pct")`.** None
would survive a committee on its own merits. Together they take a school
from **43% full to 94%**.

And the honest cost: **segregation rises**,
`r sprintf("%.3f", st(1,"seg"))` to `r sprintf("%.3f", st(4,"seg"))`.
:::

::: key-finding
But a disadvantaged child ends up travelling
**`r sprintf("%.1f", abs(st(4,"dep")))` minutes *less*** than everyone
else, where today they travel **`r sprintf("%.1f", st(1,"dep"))` minutes
more**.

Absence is this city's biggest attainment problem, and **distance is one
of the few things policy can actually change about it.**
:::
:::::
:::::::

# So what? {background-color="#17204d"}

## One person with a model is not collective intelligence {.smaller}

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="54%"}
What exists now is **a working simulation of the city's school system
that anyone can open and argue with** — councillors, officers, heads,
governors, parents.

That is necessary. It is nowhere near sufficient.

**Three things still stand in the way:**

- **Awareness.** Almost nobody (apart from you and the Council) affected knows it exists (yet).
- **Buy-in.** It only helps if the people who decide will use it.
- **Enough ideas.** A simulator is only as good as the range of
  scenarios people think to put through it — and I can only think of my
  own.
:::

:::: {.column width="46%"}
::: key-finding
**The ask.**

**Council or school?** Put a scenario through it that you think will
embarrass the model. That is genuinely the most useful thing anyone can
do with it.

**Researcher?** The code, data and model are open. Take it apart.

**Parent or governor?** Use it *before* the next consultation, not
after.
:::

The simulator does not tell the city what to do. It makes it ***much harder to claim a policy will do something the system cannot deliver.***
::::
::::::

## The actual point {.smaller}

::::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
Schools are just the example I happened to fall into.

The pattern is everywhere in any city:

- a decision that affects thousands of people,
- taken **one option at a time**,
- argued about with **anecdote and assertion**,
- where the data to do better **already exists and is published**,
- and where nobody had the time or the tools to put it together.

Road schemes and traffic filters. A leisure centre. Parking. Housing allocation. Bus routes. Waste collection. The waterfront.
:::

::::: {.column width="48%"}
::: key-finding
The cost of building a model like this has fallen by something like **an order of magnitude in about eighteen months**.

Which means the binding constraint is no longer money, or time, or
expertise.

**It is knowing which question to ask.**
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.84em; margin-top:0.9rem;"}
That is a question a room full of people is far better at than one
person — which is exactly the problem I want to finish on.
:::
:::::
:::::::

# The next problem {background-color="#1f4599"}

## The bottleneck has moved again {.smaller}

::::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
Building the model is no longer the hard part. Neither is the data — it
was published all along.

**The hard part is *when* in the process the evidence arrives.**

A consultation, more or less everywhere, runs like this:

1.  An authority decides what it wants to do.
2.  It writes the option up, with a shortlist built to make it look
    reasonable.
3.  It consults. Responses are **counted**, not modelled.
4.  It proceeds, having demonstrated that it asked.

Nobody in that sequence is acting in bad faith. It is simply a process
designed to **test consent**, not to **test options**.
:::

::::: {.column width="48%"}
::: key-finding
Which is why I could do what I did. The council's own published data
contained an answer nobody had computed — not because it was hidden, but
because the process never required anyone to look.

Two years of argument about admissions in Brighton, and **absence —
the largest single factor — was not in the consultation at all.**
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.84em; margin-top:0.9rem;"}
The simulator does not fix that. It just makes the gap between "we
consulted" and "we understood" much harder to ignore.
:::
:::::
:::::::

## What would have to change {.smaller}

::::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**The model comes before the options, not after them.** Publish the
system's behaviour first, then let people generate options against it.
The order is the whole argument.

**Alternatives get tested, not just the preferred one.** A consultation
that cannot say what the rejected options would have done has not
really compared anything.

**The model is a shared object, not the authority's.** Something the
opposition, the campaign group and the local journalist can all run
themselves. A model nobody outside can attack is just an assertion with
arithmetic in it.
:::

::::: {.column width="50%"}
::: key-finding
**Why this is hard, honestly.**

- An authority that models openly may find its preferred option **fails
  in public**. There is no incentive to go looking for that.
- Capacity: most councils have no one whose job this is, and the people
  who could do it are expensive.
- Legitimacy cuts both ways. A model can be used to **close** a debate
  as easily as to open one — "the model says" is a very good way to stop
  an argument you are losing.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.84em; margin-top:0.8rem;"}
None of that is a technical problem, which is why I think it is the
interesting one.
:::
:::::
:::::::

## The thing I actually want {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="54%"}
Not better models. We have those, and they are getting cheaper by the
month.

**A deliberative process that has somewhere to put them.** One where a
citizen, a campaigner or a councillor can arrive at a consultation with
a scenario they have already run, and have it taken as seriously as the
option on the table.

That is what "collective intelligence" has to mean in practice, or it
means nothing: not a smarter machine, but a group of people who can
**argue from a shared account of how their own city works**.
:::

::: {.column width="46%"}
::: key-finding
**So the question I would put to this room:**

What would make an authority *want* to model honestly, in public, before
it has decided?

I genuinely do not know. I suspect the answer is less about technology
than about who gets to hold the model — and I would rather be argued
with than agreed with on this one.
:::
:::
:::::
